personas.why: The knee wave gets me past the hook. Seeing exactly why the counter went wrong is the part I'd send to a colleague.
I stay to see how 14 becomes 11. Once the ghost is explained, the marks analogy feels like a second explanation of something I already got.
The red gap makes me want to know what went wrong with the rep. When the knee turns into a graph, it feels like I've switched from a gym story to a software demo.
The joint close-up gets my attention. I'd stay for the two reps moving side by side, but the contact sheet looks like the start of a longer explanation.
I can follow one dip per rep, and the wrong answer is a nice surprise. At the fix, I'm choosing between watching the hidden leg, reading the angle and following the counter.
A knee dot turning into a rep counter is something I can imagine building. I'd save the diagram and send the 14-versus-11 bit to a project teammate.
The count has a number I can check against what actually happened. Once I hear the benchmark is his own best set, I want the result, not another analogy.
Explaining the three extra reps earns some trust. Calling one set his best raises a new question: who picked that benchmark, and on what basis?
The failure and correction make the final diagram worth saving: I can explain why the system sometimes declines to count rather than just list its steps.
The opening already gives me the rep number and a verdict. Finding out whose silhouette it is doesn't change either, so I don't wait for the second stamp.
I stay to see the opening image come back with a reason under it. Once I've read that reason, the reel feels finished; I'm not looking for a build guide.
The green double is the image I'd remember. But 'two of me' already tells me whose body it is, and 'my best set' is a small reveal for a 25-second wait.
The machine blocking the leg is a better demo than a perfect count. I'd send that sequence to another dev because it shows a specific failure and what the app does about it.
I'd replay the occluded frames against the wave. Filtering a bad pose estimate is convincing; matching the human count on one clip doesn't establish that the form verdict is right.
I'd watch both reps and pause on the final reason. I might comment on whether the difference matters: looking different from your best rep isn't automatically dangerous.
The big '14 ≠ 11' card pulls me back because I instantly get the mistake. Once the counter lands on 11, that little story feels over.
